references.text: In [ref:Apg 4:27|Acts 4:27] it is confirmed that Herod and Pontius Pilate joined forces against Jesus, God's holy servant. The early church prayed for this as a fulfillment of God's plan—that those who were previously enemies became united in their opposition to Christ.

The immediate context in [ref:Luk 23:6-11|Luke 23:6-11] describes how Pilate sent Jesus to Herod, and Herod questioned him and sent him back. This exchange of Jesus between the two rulers laid the foundation for them becoming friends.

In [ref:Sal 2:1-2|Psalm 2:1-2] it is prophesied that the kings of the earth rise up and the rulers take counsel together against the Lord and his Anointed. Herod and Pilate's joint opposition to Jesus fulfills this prophetic picture of worldly powers uniting against the Messiah.

In [ref:Apg 4:25-26|Acts 4:25-26] the early church quotes Psalm 2 and applies it directly to Herod and Pilate, as representatives of "the nations" and "the kings of the earth" who gathered against the Lord and his Anointed.

In [ref:Luk 13:1|Luke 13:1] an episode is mentioned where Pilate mixed the blood of Galileans with their sacrifices. Since Herod was tetrarch over Galilee, Pilate's interference with the Galileans may have been a source of hostility between them that was now resolved.

In [ref:Luk 23:1-5|Luke 23:1-5] the trial before Pilate is described, where the Jewish council accused Jesus. Pilate found no guilt, but the accusers' claim that Jesus stirred up the people from Galilee to Jerusalem led Pilate to send him to Herod—the event that led to reconciliation between the two.
